 National party money flowing to La. after nail-biter Senate race 
 Republicans and Democrats say statewide races are no longer an easy win for GOP candidates, and national money is moving into Louisiana 
 Republicans and Democrats say statewide races are no longer an easy win for GOP candidates, and national money is moving into Louisiana By Liam Combs Published : Nov. 12, 2026 at 5:56 PM CST | Updated : 23 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB) - After Republican Julia Letlow clinched a tight race for U.S. Senate race over Democrat Jamie Davis by just over 25,000 votes, the national Republican Party has committed to more money for down-ballot races in Louisiana.
 Republican and Democratic state leaders say that statewide races are no longer an easy win for Republican candidates after high Democratic turnout this cycle. They said money is now flowing in to either reverse or improve upon that trend.
 Landry says he helped Letlow’s campaign
 “When you look at all the carnage that happened across the country, it’s amazing that Louisiana stood tall,” Governor Jeff Landry said.
 Landry said he played an instrumental role in getting Letlow elected to the Senate by reportedly lobbying President Donald Trump for his endorsement as well as speaking with donors throughout the election cycle.
 Landry said national Republicans described the race as an easy win and sent Letlow just only $60,000 until the last few weeks before the election.
 “You got the NRSC chairman Tim Scott actually sent some money down for Julia at the last minute. I called him and said look I’m telling these races are gonna be close,” Landry said.
 Party leaders react to turnout
 Derek Babcock, chair of the State Republican Party, described Tuesday’s results as a “blue tsunami.”
 “I think they certainly got a wake up call, they realize that it’s who shows up to vote that matters, and so that’s what we keep telling everybody, you can’t take these things for granted,” Babcock said.
 Democrats cite ground effort
 Democrats attribute their turnout numbers to a ground effort in which about 400 volunteers knocked on doors and connected with voters in person across the state. No national party money was spent on Davis’ campaign, aside from a $1,000 individual party contribution.
 “Direct voter contact is what really inspires and promotes voting among your electorate,” said Randal Gaines, chair of the State Democratic Party.
 Money expected for December runoffs
 Two congressional races, for Districts 5 and 6, will move to a December runoff. Both state party leaders said their national parties have committed to sending money to Louisiana for those races.
 “They have aggressively offered support, and I think the realization is there that Louisiana Democrats are worth investing in, and the potential of turning this state around,” Gaines said.
 Republicans look at Democratic approach
 Republican strategists said they have learned from the Democrats’ turnout effort.
 Babcock said Republicans will use mail, text messaging and ads, though he acknowledged people do not like receiving them.
 “But our focus is really the grassroots, getting out to the communities, communicating with the voter and reassuring them of the necessity to get out there and vote,” Babcock said.
